title: The Largest Star in the Universe – Size Comparison
beats: Opens with the question of the largest star, then starts at Earth purely for a vague sense of scale
Smallest star-like things: Jupiter (11x wider, 317x mass of Earth) made of the same stuff as the Sun, just far less
Brown dwarfs as failed stars; thought experiment of throwing 90 Jupiters together still fails to make a star
Adding mass to a brown dwarf barely grows it, only densifies it; slow fusion makes a faint glow
Main sequence defined: core hot and dense enough to fuse hydrogen
More mass means hotter, brighter, shorter life; caveat that stars are compared at different life stages, babies vs adults
Back to the beginning: red dwarfs, smallest real stars, ~100 Jupiter masses, dim, long-lived, Barnard's Star example
Sun vs Barnard's Star: 7x mass gives ~300x brightness; Sirius, then Beta Centauri: stepping up the mass ladder
Beta Centauri stars: 20,000x Sun power, only 13x size, 20 million years of life
Poses the formula 'more massive means larger' then breaks it with R136a1: 315 solar masses but only ~30x Sun radius
Why: radiation blows away extra gas, mass cap near 150 Suns; heavy stars are rare and short-lived
Reveal of the real trick: to get biggest stars you must kill them, i.e. giant phase
Red giants: core contracts, fusion speeds, outer layers swell; Gacrux 84x radius, the Sun later 200x
Hypergiants: Pistol Star 25 Msun/300 R, Rho Cassiopeiae 40 Msun/500 R; escalating size examples
Winner unknown: size error margins for distant, self-shedding red hypergiants; ranking will change
Stephenson 2-18 as current candidate at ~2150 solar radii
Scale made tangible: 8.7 hours around it at light speed, 500 years by fastest plane, fills Saturn's orbit
Life cycle ends in supernova, gas seeds new stars; loop restarts
Replays the whole journey silently as a pure visual scale comparison

metrics.examples: about 12 named objects, growing in size and extremity, with a mass-ladder then a pivot to the giant phase
metrics.ending: Honest uncertainty about the winner, then lifecycle loop and a silent replay of the size ladder

new_moves.name: break-the-obvious-rule
new_moves.what: Build a tidy rule across several examples, ask 'is this the formula?', then show an outlier that breaks it and pivot the lesson
new_moves.evidence: 4:31 more massive means larger, then R136a1

new_moves.name: unknown-as-answer
new_moves.what: Refuses to name a winner and explains why the measurement is uncertain, treating the uncertainty as content

new_moves.name: wordless-replay
new_moves.what: Replays the full visual ladder without narration so learners consolidate the scale

theory: The video teaches a catalogue by giving it a spine: a mass ladder with a fixed per-object template, then a deliberate trap (mass does not equal size) that forces the second variable, evolutionary stage, into the model. The trap is placed right after the pattern is strongest, so the correction is felt. Honest uncertainty at the end models how scientists hold claims.
velocity: Orchestrator playbook 'ladder-then-break': run a rule across 4+ examples with a fixed template, then inject a counterexample scene
Scene builder: keep a constant per-object card (mass, radius, brightness, lifespan) so repetition is visible and the exception stands out
Voice: reserve a pause and slower beat for the counterexample, not for easy list items
Learner model: ask the learner to predict the next object's size before reveal, using the rule they just inferred
Evals: check that a lesson states its own caveats about comparison fairness (babies vs adults)
quote: failed stars, that are a huge disappointment to their moms
